en: A different path to the same destination if the usual road is blocked.
A flashing amber warning light, often used on slow or working vehicles.
An orange warning light that flashes on a vehicle to make it more noticeable.
A rear-view mirror setting that reduces glare from headlights behind you at night.
A recognised training course (often for safer driving) that insurers may treat as a discount factor.
A driving teacher officially approved to give paid lessons (ADI in the UK).
When tyres ride up on water and lose grip with the road surface.
A hand signal given by the driver to show other road users what you intend to do.
An approved place that can safely take hazardous items like car batteries.
A gearbox that changes gears for you, without a clutch pedal.
The shafts that the wheels of a vehicle or trailer turn on.
A gate or arm that can block the road when a train is coming.
Areas around the vehicle that you cannot see in your mirrors alone.
A system that warns if a vehicle is in an area you cannot see in your mirrors.
A system that warns you about vehicles in areas you cannot see in the mirrors.
Fluid-filled swellings on the skin that can form after burns; do not burst them.
A flashing blue warning light used by certain emergency or specialist vehicles.
Emergency warning lights used by police, fire, ambulance, and similar services.
The outer shell and panels of the vehicle (bonnet, wings, doors, etc.).
A short post on the road used to mark an island, edge, or obstruction.
A road junction painted with yellow criss-cross lines on the road surface.
Red lights at the rear that come on when you press the brake pedal.
When a vehicle stops working and can no longer be driven normally.
Stops working so the vehicle cannot continue normally.
Dashed white road markings, often showing a boundary you may cross when safe.
A town or village area with buildings beside the road; street lighting often marks a 30 mph zone.
Towns or villages with buildings close to the road; a 30 mph limit often applies with street lights.
When vehicles pack closely together, often causing sudden braking waves.
Lanes reserved mainly for buses (and sometimes taxis or cycles).
A trailer designed for living or camping, towed behind a vehicle.
The part of the road used by vehicles, not the pavement or verge.
People injured in an accident or emergency.
An injured person in an accident.
The strip or barrier that separates the two directions of traffic on a dual carriageway.
Repeated firm pushes on the centre of the chest during CPR to pump blood.
A child seat or similar device that holds a child safely in the vehicle.
A special seat that holds a child safely with the correct restraints.
A road marked so that stopping on the main carriageway is tightly restricted.
The pedal that disconnects the engine from the wheels so you can change gear.
Rolling along with the clutch pressed or in neutral, so the engine is not driving the wheels.
Rolling down a slope without using the engine to help control speed.
A crash when vehicles or objects hit each other.
Heavy, slow-moving traffic when roads are overcrowded.
Say or show the opposite of something else.
A temporary traffic system where vehicles travel in the opposite direction to normal, often during roadworks.
A temporary traffic system where vehicles travel in the opposite direction to normal, often during roadworks.
An area where parking is controlled by signs and marked bays at set times.
The liquid in the engine cooling system that helps stop the engine overheating.
Posts with decreasing bars (3, 2, 1) showing how close you are to a motorway exit.
A narrow rural road, often with limited space and visibility.
An extra uphill lane for slow vehicles so faster traffic is not held up.
A junction where two roads cross, usually forming a plus-sign shape.
A system that holds a set speed without keeping your foot on the accelerator.
Moves suddenly into your lane or gap with little space in front of you.
A part of the road marked for cyclists, shown by a bicycle symbol and lane lines.
A person riding a bicycle on the road.
Hazardous materials (chemicals, fuels, etc.) needing special transport rules.
A light on the instrument panel that alerts you to a vehicle fault or important status.
Temporarily blind someone with bright light.
Temporarily blinded or unable to see clearly because of bright lights.
Scattered pieces of wreckage, objects, or rubbish left after a crash.
A portable device that can deliver an electric shock to try to restart a heart in cardiac arrest.
A control that clears mist from the windows so you can see clearly.
Controls that clear mist from the windows so you can see clearly.
White diamond road markings that show a lane reserved for particular vehicles.
The cover that seals the diesel filler opening; if loose, fuel can spill onto the road.
Switch from full beam to dipped (lower) beam so oncoming or overtaking drivers are not dazzled.
